newsitem.title: JAPAN: WEEK AHEAD-Japan stocks seen hovering, eyes on yen.
newsitem.headline: WEEK AHEAD-Japan stocks seen hovering, eyes on yen.

text.p: Tokyo stocks are seen hovering this week ahead of the G7 summit in Denver, with attention focused on currencies, brokers said.
Trading, however, was likely to be robust, helped by pension fund allocations, they said. They expect the market's downside will likely be at the 20,000 level.

"There is speculation that a vast amount of funds will come to the market via trust banks and investment trusts," said Katsuhiko Kodama, general manager at Toyo Securities. "Stock futures have been surging lately in anticipation of the great demand."

Kiyoshi Kimura of Societe Generale Securities said buying by pension and public funds would not generate rises as these funds usually do not chase the indices higher and tend to wait for dips to emerge before going into the market.
Analysts forecast a range of 20,150 to 20,800 for the key Nikkei 225 average this week.

On Friday, the benchmark finished 36.11 points or 0.18 percent lower at 20,528.35. It hit 20,815.48 at one stage helped by the June futures and options settlement, surpassing its previous 1997 high of 20,707.77 set on June 4.
Brokers said any rises could be capped by investors moving to the sidelines, wary of turbulence in currencies ahead of the June 20-22 summit.

In the past week, currencies have been volatile "on worries over Japan's trade surplus and until the summit, a clear direction will probably not appear for the yen", said Yamaichi Securities general manager Katsumichi Shimizu.

The yen yo-yoed wildly after the announcement that Japan's April current account surplus had jumped 92.7 percent from the previous year, which raised concerns over Japan's trade surplus ahead of the G7 summit meeting.
"As long as the yen does not keep powering beyond 110, yen exporters will be all right," said Mitsuru Hayashino, Sanyo Securities general manager.
Brokers said attention would continue to be on foreign investors, who have been the only net buyers in the Japanese stock market in recent weeks.

Apart from foreign-investor buying on the back of a rise in the Dow industrials, brokers said funds could shift from the European market amid mounting political and economic questions over the future of European economic and monetary union.

"The indices are likely to be in a tug of war between foreign investors who are keen on buying and domestic institutional investors who are taking profits," a general manager at Daiwa Securities said.
